drills.q: A stakeholder asks why you don't just use one large model end-to-end instead of the retrieval-ranking-reranking pipeline. What's the technical answer?
drills.a: No single model can simultaneously be cheap enough to score millions-to-billions of items within a real-time latency budget AND rich enough for genuine cross-features -- these requirements are in direct tension. The funnel resolves this by applying a cheap high-recall model to the full catalog, reserving the expensive high-precision model for only the small candidate set retrieval narrowed down to.

drills.q: A two-tower retrieval model's top candidates look topically relevant but miss a known user-item-specific signal (e.g. 'user always buys this brand during this promotion'). Diagnose.
drills.a: This is the expected structural limitation of two-tower architecture -- towers never see each other's features, interacting only via a final dot product, so genuine cross-features can't be captured at retrieval. Verify the downstream ranking stage (which CAN see cross-features) is correctly re-scoring and promoting these cases; don't expect retrieval-stage recall to reflect this signal.

drills.q: A LambdaMART ranking model shows strong offline NDCG but the online A/B test is flat or negative. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: Selection bias in logged data -- historical logs only show outcomes for items the previous policy already chose to show, so offline metrics implicitly evaluate re-ranking of already-selected items, not the full candidate distribution. Use counterfactual/off-policy evaluation (e.g. inverse propensity weighting) where possible, and always confirm with an online A/B test before a significant launch.

drills.q: Why would naively binarizing implicit feedback and running explicit-rating MF on it produce a biased model?
drills.a: It treats every non-interaction as a confident negative rating, conflating 'saw it and disliked it' with 'never saw it at all' -- for most catalogs the vast majority of zero cells are the latter, so this systematically biases the model against low-exposure items and users regardless of true preference.

drills.q: You're launching a new product category with zero historical interaction data inside an existing mature recommendation system. Walk through the end-to-end cold-start handling.
drills.a: Retrieval: fall back to content-based similarity (metadata/pretrained embeddings, no collaborative signal yet) for likely-interested users based on other-category behavior. Ranking: blend a popularity/content-relevance prior with early weak collaborative signal, increasing CF weight as interaction count grows. Layer explicit exploration via a contextual bandit to accelerate data accumulation, and monitor the rate of items crossing a 'sufficient interaction' threshold as a leading indicator for phasing down cold-start treatment.

drills.q: How would you decide whether a deep cross-feature neural ranker is worth its added complexity over a well-tuned LambdaMART model for a specific ranking problem?
drills.a: Run both on the same feature set and data, and check whether the deep model's gain is concentrated in patterns genuinely hard to hand-engineer (e.g. long user-behavior sequences) versus patterns a few additional cross-features would let LambdaMART capture just as well at much lower serving cost. If cheap feature engineering closes most of the gap, that's usually the better investment than switching architectures.

drills.q: Your cold-start exploration budget (contextual bandit traffic to new items) -- how do you know if it's too large or too small?
drills.a: Track the overall business metric (revenue, engagement) with and without the exploration allocation via a held-out control group, and separately track the rate at which new items accumulate sufficient interaction data to exit cold-start status. A sustained hit to the business metric signals reducing/targeting the budget; a too-slow graduation rate despite reasonable budget suggests an exposure/impression problem rather than a ranking-model problem.

drills.q: ALS training scales well with more users/items in Spark but convergence quality degrades on a very sparse, heavy long-tail catalog. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Extremely sparse rows leave many items/users with too few observed interactions for a stable per-row least-squares solve, even with L2 regularization -- V_obs^T V_obs can be poorly conditioned with very few observations. Fix: increase lambda for sparse rows specifically, use a hybrid content+CF model for the long tail, or apply a minimum-interaction-count filter before including an entity in pure CF training.
